title: Towards Text-Mask Consistency in Medical Image Segmentation
one_liner: Segment medical images by fixing the link between the written finding and the predicted mask, so the highlighted region matches what the report actually says.
lead: Medical image segmentation marks the pixels that belong to a lesion, organ, or other target region. In a vision-language setting, the model should use both the image and a text description, such as a finding report or lesion prompt. The failure is that many systems produce a mask that does not fully agree with the text, especially when the text mentions several sites or several lesions. One reason is pretraining: medical reports reuse many phrases, so standard contrastive learning treats many semantically similar reports as negatives and pushes their representations apart even when they describe the same condition. Another reason is fusion: many models let vision dominate the cross-modal interaction, so text features do not get a strong path into the spatial prediction. C2Seg fixes both problems. It softens the contrastive targets so similar reports are not treated as hard negatives, and it adds a two-way attention block (a module that lets image features and text features reweight one another) where each modality guides the other in its own branch. That matters because the segmentation mask should not only cover plausible anatomy. It should cover the anatomy described by the text.

problem.h2: A good-looking mask can still contradict the report
paras: In medical segmentation, the output is a mask: a yes-or-no decision for each pixel about whether that pixel belongs to the target. If the text says 'two lesions in the right lung' and the mask highlights one lesion on the left, the system failed even if the highlighted shape looks medically plausible. The problem is not only image understanding. It is agreement between the spatial output and the written description.

Two technical choices create the mismatch. First, standard contrastive pretraining pairs each image with its own report and pushes it away from all other reports in the batch. That assumption is too harsh for clinical language because many reports use nearly identical wording for similar findings. Pushing those reports apart damages cross-modal alignment, because the model is told that a semantically similar report should be treated as unrelated. Second, one-way fusion lets image features pull from text features, but it does not give text a strong route to shape the spatial map. The segmentation head therefore stays mostly vision-driven even when the text contains the disambiguating detail.

callout.html: Use softer text supervision during pretraining and bidirectional fusion during segmentation, because the model must preserve medical meaning and inject that meaning into the pixel grid.

steps.text: Encode the medical image and the accompanying report or prompt into feature sets used by the segmentation model.
Use a frozen strong baseline to estimate which reports in the batch are semantically similar, so those pairs are not treated as hard negatives.
Train contrastively with the soft targets, so the visual features stay compatible with several medically related text descriptions.
Run bidirectional attention where image-guided fusion and text-guided fusion both contribute to the joint feature map.

steps.b: Gate the fused features and predict a mask
steps.text: Use the attention gate to strengthen useful multimodal patterns before the decoder turns them into pixel labels.

paras: C2Seg changes both the pretraining target and the fusion path. It replaces one-to-one contrastive supervision with cluster-aware soft supervision, and it replaces mostly one-way cross-modal fusion with a two-path design where language has its own spatially relevant route into the segmentation features.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: semantic conflict inside the batch
hidden.name: How often the training loss says two similar reports should be pushed apart
paras: The paper is really controlling semantic conflict in the contrastive loss. In a standard batch, every non-matching text is a negative example. In medical data, that rule is often wrong because many reports differ in patient identity or minor wording but describe the same anatomy or lesion type. When the loss pushes those reports apart, it teaches the image encoder that medically related findings should live far from each other in feature space.

Cluster-aware contrastive learning reduces that conflict by using soft similarity labels. A report that is very similar to the anchor report gets a mild penalty or no penalty instead of the full negative push. This matters because the model should reserve its separation power for genuinely different findings, not for near-duplicates created by clinical writing style.

heat.caption: Darker means the batch relation helps learning. Low values mark pairings where the loss would create a misleading separation.

reads.html: The bad case is when two reports mean nearly the same thing but the training rule treats one as evidence against the other, because that damages the image-text link.

The soft similarity matrix (a table of report-to-report similarity scores) reduces false negatives in contrastive learning, so the learned representation preserves medically correct closeness among related reports because similar findings are no longer pushed apart as if they were opposites.

mechanism.h2: Why softer alignment and two-way fusion fix the mismatch
paras: Contrastive pretraining is supposed to make matching image-text pairs close and non-matching pairs far apart. That works when non-matching pairs are truly unrelated. In medical language, that assumption breaks because the reports are repetitive. If two reports both describe a small right-lung lesion, pushing them apart tells the model that shared medical content is not important. C2Seg replaces the hard rule with a graded rule, so similar reports stay partly compatible. The result is a visual encoder that preserves medical semantics instead of learning arbitrary distinctions caused by phrasing.

The second fix is inside segmentation. A mask is spatial, so text has to influence which image locations become active. In one-way fusion, text often acts only as a weak modifier on top of strong image features. C2Seg gives each modality a dominant branch: one branch starts from image structure and pulls in text, while the other starts from text meaning and projects it into spatial features. That second path matters because the report can specify count, side, or lesion identity that is not obvious from shape alone.

The gate on top of the fused features matters because not every cross-modal interaction is useful. The gate raises the weight of feature combinations that consistently support the described target and lowers the weight of combinations that mix unrelated image regions with text tokens. The decoder then receives a feature map that is already filtered toward text-consistent spatial evidence.

math.words: The method adds a soft-label contrastive loss to the segmentation loss, so alignment and pixel prediction are trained together.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one image report says 'two liver lesions' and another says 'multiple lesions in the liver dome.'
A hard contrastive loss would treat the second report as fully negative for the first image, even though their meanings overlap.
The soft-label loss assigns partial similarity instead, so the first image is not pushed far from the second report.
Later, when the segmentation head reads the phrase about lesion count and location, the fused features still carry that meaning.
That is why the final mask is more likely to cover the lesions named by the report instead of a generic suspicious region.

math.note: The exact shape of the soft loss can vary. The important part is that medical text similarity changes the penalty, so the model does not learn from false opposition, because reports with overlapping meaning no longer act as full-strength negatives.

bars.h2: What changes when text really reaches the mask

charts.title: Hard negatives plus one-way fusion
charts.note: The model can locate plausible tissue, but it often misses the exact site or lesion count named in the text because alignment and fusion are both weak.

charts.title: C2Seg
charts.note: Better pretraining and stronger language-to-space fusion help the system follow the written description while keeping the mask anatomically valid, because the pretraining stage preserves report meaning and the fusion stage carries that meaning into the spatial map.

items.b: The soft similarity labels are wrong.
items.html: If the frozen baseline says two reports are similar when they actually refer to different findings, the model will keep incompatible cases too close. That weakens the contrastive signal because real negatives stop being separated.
If the report does not clearly name the target region, no fusion rule can force the right mask. The image branch will dominate because the text provides too little disambiguating information.

If the language branch injects broad activation (strong responses across many image locations) without enough spatial precision, the model may light up too many candidate areas because the wording is medically relevant but not tightly localized.
Use reliable soft similarity estimates, reports with enough detail, and a fusion module that preserves spatial structure. Then the text supplies meaning and the image supplies localization.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a segmentation benchmark where each image comes with a short target description and a ground-truth mask. Include cases with multiple lesions and mirrored anatomy, because those cases expose text-mask mismatch clearly. Compare a hard-negative contrastive baseline against C2Seg. For each prediction, score not only overlap with the ground-truth mask but also agreement with text facts such as side, count, and named structure. The demo should show that C2Seg reduces cases where the mask is medically plausible yet semantically wrong.
demo.closing: The target result is a mask that obeys the report. A pure overlap score is not enough if the highlighted region contradicts the words.
